title: The Unit Circle and Radians
objectives: Convert between degrees and radians and explain why radians are the natural unit
Locate points on the unit circle and state sine and cosine as coordinates
Evaluate trig functions at any angle using reference angles and quadrant sign rules
Interpret amplitude, period and midline in a sinusoidal model of a price or liquidity cycle
motivation: Prices cycle: intraday liquidity breathes, weekly effects repeat, oscillators swing. Sine and cosine are the mathematics of anything periodic, and the unit circle is the machine that generates them, an angle goes in, a point comes out. Radians, the natural angular unit, make arc length a multiplication and will make the calculus of sines clean in later phases. This lesson connects the triangle ratios you just learned to the circle they secretly live on.

blocks.md: Degrees chop a circle into 360 arbitrary pieces, a historical accident inherited from Babylonian astronomy. A **radian** is defined by the circle itself: it is the angle that subtends an arc equal in length to the radius. One full turn is therefore $2\pi$ radians (circumference $2\pi r$ over radius $r$), half a turn is $180^\circ = \pi$, and arc length becomes plain multiplication: $s = r\theta$ with $\theta$ in radians. That naturalness is not cosmetic, in later calculus, identities like $(\sin x)' = \cos x$ are true only in radians, so standard functions such as Python math.sin take radians; always check the actual API contract.

A useful way to avoid errors is to stop treating the unit circle only as a lookup table and view it as a machine. The machine view: an angle is a **distance walked** counter-clockwise from $(1, 0)$ along a circle of radius 1. Walk $\pi/2$ and you land on $(0, 1)$. Walk $\pi$ and you are at $(-1, 0)$. Walk $2\pi$ and you are home again. Sine and cosine are just the coordinates of wherever you stopped, which is why $\sin(\theta + 2\pi) = \sin(\theta)$ is not a formula to memorise: nothing stops you from continuing to walk.

Every sign rule you ever struggled with dissolves here. In which quadrant is $\sin(7\pi/6)$ negative? You have walked just past $\pi$, so you are **below** the x-axis and to the left of the origin, the third quadrant. Height (sine) is negative, x-position (cosine) is negative. No mnemonic needed; you can *see* it. This also explains the periodic structure of financial models: any model built on $\sin(\omega t)$ is a model of something that walks the circle at speed $\omega$, and phase is just where on the circle you started.

blocks.title: Radians are the honest unit
blocks.md: On a unit circle, a positive angle in radians equals its subtended arc length. The small-angle relation sin(h)/h approaches 1 only for radian h. If the input variable is in degrees, differentiating sin(pi*x/180) gives(pi/180)*cos(pi*x/180): the calculus is valid with the conversion factor. Use degrees or radians deliberately rather than leaving one calculator mode fixed for every problem.

The last piece of fluency is walking **backwards** (clockwise, negative angles) and beyond one lap (angles above $2\pi$). $\cos(-\theta) = \cos(\theta)$ because walking backwards lands you at the mirror position across the x-axis, same x-coordinate, negated height, hence $\sin(-\theta) = -\sin(\theta)$. These symmetries let you reduce any angle to a reference angle in $[0, \pi/2]$, which is how numerical libraries evaluate trig functions cheaply and how you should sanity-check them by hand.

blocks.title: Worked conversions and an arc length
items: One radian $\approx 57.2958^\circ$ - a bit under a sixth of a full turn.
If the radius is 2 metres and theta=1.5 radians, the arc length is s=2*1.5=3 metres. It is not 3 radius-lengths, which would be6 metres.
The ratio arc length/radius is dimensionless, but arc length retains the same length unit as radius. Radians simplify angular formulas; they do not remove physical unit bookkeeping.

blocks.text: The unit circle as a function machine

blocks.md: Walk anticlockwise around a radius-1 circle starting at $(1, 0)$. After turning through angle $\theta$ you stand at the point $(\cos\theta, \sin\theta)$: the $x$-coordinate **is** cosine, the $y$-coordinate **is** sine. This single picture explains everything at once: values repeat every $2\pi$ (**periodicity**); sine and cosine trade places a quarter-turn apart; and their signs rotate through the quadrants, both positive in Q1, only sine in Q2, only tangent in Q3 (two negatives), only cosine in Q4. The triangle ratios of the last lesson were the circle seen from one corner.

blocks.title: Worked example: reference angles
items: $\sin 150^\circ$: 150 degrees sits in Q2; its reference angle is $180^\circ - 150^\circ = 30^\circ$; sine stays positive in Q2, so $\sin 150^\circ = \sin 30^\circ = 1/2$.
Strategy for any angle: reduce to the reference angle, then apply the quadrant's sign rule.

blocks.caption: y = sin(x) over one full period on each side of zero: the unit circle unrolled onto a graph. Every 2pi the pattern repeats.

blocks.text: Periodicity in the market: a price cycle

blocks.title: Worked example: a 40-day cycle
items: Model a cyclical price as $p(t) = 100 + 4\sin\left(\frac{2\pi t}{40}\right)$, with $t$ in days: midline 100, amplitude 4, period 40 days.
At $t = 10$: the argument is $2\pi(10)/40 = \pi/2$, where $\sin = 1$, so $p = 104$ - the top of the swing.
At $t = 20$: argument $= \pi$, $\sin = 0$, $p = 100$; at $t = 30$: argument $= 3\pi/2$, $\sin = -1$, $p = 96$ - the bottom.
The factor $2\pi/40$ converts days into turns of the circle: one full cycle per 40 days.

blocks.title: Cycles everywhere
blocks.md: Some market activity has daily or seasonal patterns, but not every observed cycle is sinusoidal or stable. Under suitable regularity assumptions, Fourier series represent periodic signals using sine and cosine modes. A fitted cycle is a model to test out of sample, not evidence that prices must repeat.

blocks.title: Mode matters
blocks.md: sin(30) is 0.5 when 30 denotes degrees, but Python math.sin(30) treats 30 as radians and is about-0.988. Other APIs can provide degree-based functions. Check the function contract and use an explicit conversion, such as math.radians(30), when needed.

guidedExercise.prompt: Evaluate $\cos 225^\circ$ and $\sin(4\pi/3)$ using reference angles, stating the quadrant of each angle.
hints: 225 degrees is in Q3; its reference angle is $225^\circ - 180^\circ$.
In Q3 both sine and cosine are negative; tangent is positive.
guidedExercise.solution: $\cos 225^\circ$: reference angle $45^\circ$, cosine negative in Q3, so $-\sqrt{2}/2 \approx -0.7071$. $\sin(4\pi/3) = \sin 240^\circ$: reference angle $60^\circ$, sine negative in Q3, so $-\sqrt{3}/2 \approx -0.8660$.
guidedExercise.successCheck: Both angles are in quadrantIII. Cos 225 degrees=-sqrt(2)/2 and sin(4pi/3)=-sqrt(3)/2; the signs and magnitudes match their unit-circle coordinates.

independentExercise.prompt: A hypothetical 24-hour market activity measure is modelled as $L(t) = 50 + 20\sin\left(\frac{\pi t}{12}\right)$ (units: \$ millions of quote volume per minute), with $t$ the hours from midnight. (a) State the amplitude and period. (b) Compute $L(6)$ and $L(18)$. (c) At what times is liquidity exactly at the midline of 50? Restrict part(c) to the closed interval 0<=t<=24; this illustrative sinusoid is not a claim about real market opening hours or a universal U-shaped volume profile.
hints: Compare $\pi t/12$ with the general form $2\pi t/T$ to read off the period.
The sine term is 0 at arguments $0, \pi, 2\pi$.
independentExercise.solution: (a) Amplitude 20; since $\pi t/12 = 2\pi t/24$, the period is 24 hours. (b) $L(6) = 50 + 20\sin(\pi/2) = 70$ - the peak at 06:00; $L(18) = 50 + 20\sin(3\pi/2) = 30$ - the trough at 18:00. (c) $\sin = 0$ at $0, \pi, 2\pi$, i.e. $t = 0, 12, 24$: midnight, noon and the next midnight.
independentExercise.successCheck: Amplitude 20 and period 24 hours, with L(6)=70 and L(18)=30. On0<=t<=24, the midline crossings are 0,12,24 only.

commonMistakes: Using degree values where radians are expected (or vice versa), always check the mode or the API contract.
Dropping the quadrant sign: $\sin 150^\circ$ and $\sin 30^\circ$ share a magnitude but live in different quadrants.
Treating $\tan 90^\circ$ as a large number rather than undefined (cosine is zero there).
Reading the period of $\sin(2\pi t/40)$ as 40 radians instead of 40 time units, keep track of what $t$ measures.
realWorldApplication: Radians simplify standard rotation, wave and arc-length formulas. Many engineering systems are modelled using angles or periodic components, but their exact units and physical assumptions still need to be stated.
quantFinanceApplication: Periodic market structure, intraday liquidity cycles, seasonal demand, oscillator indicators, is modelled with sinusoids; the amplitude/period/midline parameters here are exactly what seasonal-regression models estimate on real price data.
summary: Radians define angle by arc: one turn is $2\pi$ rad, $180^\circ = \pi$, and arc length is $s = r\theta$.
On the unit circle, angle $\theta$ lands on the point $(\cos\theta, \sin\theta)$; values repeat with period $2\pi$.
Evaluate any angle via its reference angle plus the quadrant sign rule (Q1 all positive, Q2 sine, Q3 tangent, Q4 cosine).
A nonconstant sinusoid p(t)=D+A*sin(2pi*t/T), with T>0, has midlineD, amplitude|A| and periodT. It is one possible model for periodic data, not every cyclical process.

quiz.prompt: Convert 270 degrees to radians as a decimal rounded to two places.
quiz.explanation: Multiply a degree measure by pi/180:270*pi/180=3pi/2, about 4.71239 radians or4.71 to two places. A full turn is 360 degrees=2pi radians, so this is three-quarters of a turn.
150 degrees is in Q2 with reference angle 30 degrees; sine is positive there, so $\sin 150^\circ = 1/2$.

quiz.prompt: A circle has radius 2 metres and a positive angle 1.5 radians. What is the subtended arc length in metres?
quiz.explanation: Arc length is radius times radian angle:2 metres*1.5=3 metres. The angle is the ratio of arc length to radius, so radians are dimensionless while the result retains the radius length unit. Degrees would require conversion before this multiplication.

quiz.prompt: With the price model $p(t) = 100 + 4\sin(2\pi t/40)$, what is $p(30)$?
quiz.explanation: At t=30 days the argument is 2pi*30/40=3pi/2. Sine is-1 there, so the model gives 100-4=96, its minimum. The midline is 100 and the amplitude is 4; this is a hypothetical deterministic cycle, not a price forecast.

quiz.prompt: What does this Python script print?
quiz.explanation: math.radians converts 150 degrees to $5\pi/6$, giving 0.5. But math.sin(30) treats 30 as radians: $\sin 30 \approx -0.988$ - the mode trap.

quiz.prompt: Why do mathematics and numerical libraries prefer radians over degrees?
quiz.modelAnswer: A radian is defined by arc equal to radius, so s = r-theta holds by multiplication and derivatives like (sin x)' = cos x are true only when angles are in radians.
quiz.explanation: Radians make arc length multiplicative and keep the calculus clean, the derivative of sine is cosine only in radians.

quiz.prompt: What are the unit-circle coordinates at angle 2pi/3, in(x,y) order?
quiz.explanation: Unit-circle coordinates are(cos(theta),sin(theta)). The angle 120 degrees is in quadrantII with reference angle 60 degrees, so cosine=-1/2 and sine=sqrt(3)/2. Swapping sine and cosine would reverse the coordinate roles.

quiz.prompt: For p(t)=100+4sin(2pi*t/40), which parameter statements are correct?
options: The period is 40 days when t is in days
All observed asset prices must follow this cycle
quiz.explanation: The added constant sets the midline, the magnitude of the sine coefficient sets amplitude, and 2pi divided by angular frequency 2pi/40 gives 40 days. These parameters describe the stated model, not a universal law for observed asset prices.

flashcards.back: $180^\circ = \pi$ radians; multiply degrees by $\pi/180$ to convert.
The angle subtending an arc equal in length to the radius; one full turn is $2\pi$ radians.
At angle $\theta$ the point is $(\cos\theta, \sin\theta)$; values repeat with period $2\pi$.
Reduce any angle to its acute angle with the x-axis, then apply the quadrant's sign rule to get sine and cosine.
